clue.text: Outspoken characters poke fun at cocky individual

indicators.note: outspoken here means spoken out loud, so the letters named are taken by their sound

parts.note: two Y characters, said out loud
to guy someone is to mock them

explanation.surface: People with sharp tongues tease a swaggering show-off.
explanation.walkthrough: Ys spoken sounds like WISE; 'characters' are letters of the alphabet, not people.
explanation.definitionFit: A wise guy is a smart alec, someone brash and overconfident who thinks he knows better.

clue.text: See 9 Across
Boozer, bum

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a heavy drinker who soaks it up
second meaning: to cadge or scrounge from others

explanation.surface: A curt dismissal of a drunk layabout.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two nouns describing one person, but the second word is a verb meaning to scrounge.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang calls a heavy drinker this, and as a verb it means to live off other people's generosity.

clue.text: Visits daughter and breaks down

parts.note: to visit someone is to go to see them
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: Someone calls on their daughter and becomes overcome with emotion.
explanation.definitionFit: To run to seed is to deteriorate or decline through neglect, as an untended plant bolts.

clue.text: Tough lad put up with the same cut

indicators.note: in a down clue, put up means written bottom to top
cut means trimmed, so the word loses its tail letter

explanation.surface: A hard young man had his hair cut in the same style.
explanation.walkthrough: The second BOY loses its last letter. 'Tough' is a noun here: a thug.
explanation.definitionFit: A yobbo is British slang for a loutish young hooligan, the sort of person also called a tough.

clue.text: Fragrant ingredient ending on tongue in mouth, say, not a sausage!

indicators.note: one thing placed in another, so the first letter goes inside the second word

parts.note: the mouth is an example of an organ of the body
not a sausage is British slang for nothing at all, which is zero

explanation.surface: A cook complains there is no sausage, only a fragrant flavour left lingering on the tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: E sits inside ORGAN, then O is added. 'Not a sausage' is British slang for nothing whatsoever.
explanation.definitionFit: Oregano is an aromatic herb used widely in Italian and Greek cooking.

clue.text: Running, then changing pace, nothing ahead

indicators.note: changing means the word's letters are rearranged
ahead places the zero at the very front of everything else

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O
a trot is a pace of a horse

explanation.surface: A runner speeds up, then changes pace, with nothing in front of them.
explanation.definitionFit: On the trot is British idiom for in succession, one after another, as wins run consecutively.

clue.text: Pipe hasn't opened in vessel

indicators.note: something that has not opened is missing its opening, so the word loses its front letter

parts.note: a sewer is a large underground drainage pipe

explanation.surface: A blocked pipe has failed to open inside some container.
explanation.walkthrough: SEWER drops its first letter S. 'Hasn't opened' reads like a stuck valve but means the opening letter is gone.
explanation.definitionFit: A ewer is a large jug with a wide mouth, a container for carrying water.

clue.text: Earlier version once with star performing

indicators.note: performing suggests the words are acting out new roles in a different arrangement

explanation.surface: An older production of a show that once featured a celebrity in the cast.
explanation.definitionFit: A forerunner or prototype from which later forms developed is described as their ancestor.

clue.text: Single unit impressing soldier, five-hundred marching up and down

indicators.note: impressing means pressing something into the first word, which holds it

explanation.surface: A lone army unit makes an impression on a soldier while five hundred troops march to and fro.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Impressing' means pressing into: the soldier and the numeral go inside the single unit, before its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Troops drilled on parade march in formation back and forth across a square.

clue.text: Worn like a pair of jeans, best one, was he describing trousers?

definitions.text: Worn like a pair of jeans

indicators.note: to trouser is to pocket, so the phrase pockets the answer within it

parts.note: run across the words, ignoring spaces

explanation.surface: A question about someone praising the finest pair of trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' looks like a noun about clothing, but it is a verb: pockets, holds inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Denim is given a faded, worn appearance by being tumbled with pumice during manufacture.

clue.text: With carnation originally pressed, flatter flower

indicators.note: pressed in means squeezed inside the following phrase

parts.note: to butter up is to flatter

indicators.note: originally means at its origin, the first letter only

explanation.surface: Someone pressing a carnation between pages flattens one flower beside another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flatter' looks like a comparative of flat, the surface sense of pressed flowers, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The buttercup is a common yellow wild flower of fields and meadows.

clue.text: Oxford and Cambridge, for example, might see various houses like that

indicators.note: houses means holds inside, so the shuffled letters hold a short word
various means the two words are rearranged into a different order

explanation.surface: Oxford and Cambridge might be seen in different college houses.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the two Boat Race crews, each a rowing eight, not the universities as places.
explanation.definitionFit: Each Boat Race boat carries eight oarsmen, so each crew is a group of eight people.

clue.text: Ruler that's serving as ruler, primarily

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so only the leading letter of each word counts

parts.note: the first letters of these four words

explanation.surface: A riddle about whoever is acting as monarch in the first place.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'ruler' appears twice: the first is the definition, the second is just a source of its own initial letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsar was the emperor of Russia, an absolute monarch.

clue.text: A miscue in rough after possible selection of driver?

indicators.note: a miscue is a mishit, so the words that follow come out wrong and jumbled

explanation.surface: A golfer mishits from the rough after choosing a driver club.
explanation.walkthrough: The golf scene makes driver a club; really it is someone at the wheel of a car.
explanation.definitionFit: A motorist shifting through a gearbox might choose this ratio when cruising.

clue.text: Seat and doors go around — it seems to be working

indicators.note: going around means the letters are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: Furniture and doors are being moved around a room, and the arrangement seems to work.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is said when progress has been satisfactory up to now, implying things are going well.

clue.text: Wearing down iron, heat affected rust

indicators.note: affected means altered, so the word's letters are disturbed

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: Iron gradually wears away as heat speeds up corrosion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wearing down' suggests erosion, but down is soft plumage, and wearing it means being covered in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird clad in soft plumage has feathers on, so it is literally wearing its down.

clue.text: Aligned, paintings etc put up — where visible?

indicators.note: where visible is in view, and the in places the first word inside
in a down clue, put up means written from bottom to top

parts.note: paintings and so on are art

explanation.surface: Pictures are hung level on a wall, but where can they be seen?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Where visible?' is read as 'in sight', and its 'in' tells you to put the reversed art inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lined up evenly, with no bend or tilt, is straight.

clue.text: Ralph has come up with duck in gravy — wonderful!

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means being read from bottom to top

parts.note: to ralph is slang for to vomit

indicators.note: in places the first word inside the second

parts.note: jus is a thin meat gravy
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket

explanation.surface: Ralph has been sick after eating duck in gravy, and someone finds it marvellous.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb is reversed, then O goes inside JUS. Frabjous is Lewis Carroll's coinage from 'Jabberwocky'.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll invented the word as a joyful exclamation meaning splendid or delightful.

clue.text: Prime minister's initial bloomer — something that would float?

indicators.note: initial means the first letter only of the word it follows

parts.note: an aster is a flower, something that blooms

explanation.surface: A head of government's first blunder, perhaps a policy floated before it sank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prime minister' reads as one office but splits: Prime is a number, minister supplies only its M. A bloomer is British slang for a blunder, but here it is a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: A three-master is a sailing ship with three masts, and ships are made to float.

clue.text: Fascist leader in Italy clued cryptically

indicators.note: something written cryptically is disguised, here by scrambling the letters

parts.note: I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: A dictator in Italy is described in a riddling way.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a plain statement about Italian history while the wordplay sits in plain view.
explanation.definitionFit: Mussolini styled himself by this Italian title, meaning the leader, as dictator of Fascist Italy.

clue.text: Canine with crown on basically like every tooth

indicators.note: the crown is the top, so in a down clue the head letter of that word is taken

parts.note: all of the teeth form a set

explanation.surface: A dog's tooth with a crown fitted, much like every other tooth it has.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canine' looks like a tooth in this dental scene; it is the dog.
explanation.definitionFit: The basset hound is a short-legged breed of dog with long drooping ears.

clue.text: A King of blues accompanies a pop group

parts.note: B.B. King was a famous blues guitarist

explanation.surface: A blues legend performs alongside a pop band.
explanation.definitionFit: The Swedish quartet behind 'Waterloo' and 'Dancing Queen' were among the best-selling pop acts ever.

clue.text: Nip by jaw on a furry animal

parts.note: the chin is the front of the lower jaw
a nip in the air is a chill

explanation.surface: A small pet bites someone's jaw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nip' suggests a bite, but it is cold weather.
explanation.definitionFit: The chinchilla is a small Andean rodent prized for its dense, very soft fur.

clue.text: A little glutton ate seventeen buns

indicators.note: a little means a small part of the following words is taken

parts.note: run across the words, ignoring spaces

explanation.surface: A small greedy eater devoured seventeen bread rolls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buns' looks like baked goods in this eating scene; it is slang for the buttocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Nates is the anatomical Latin term for the buttocks, which American slang calls buns.

clue.text: Herbivore's wish upon a star

parts.note: a plant-eater wants vegetables, veg for short

explanation.surface: A plant-eating animal makes a wish on a star, as in the song.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer, 'upon' places the first piece on top of the second. The surface borrows 'When You Wish Upon a Star'.
explanation.definitionFit: Vega is the brightest star in the constellation Lyra, one of the brightest in the night sky.

clue.text: Travel bag, into which throw rubbish

indicators.note: into which means the next word is put inside the one just named

parts.note: to bag something is to get it

explanation.surface: A travel bag is something you toss your junk into.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bag' looks like luggage, but it is a verb: to catch or obtain.
explanation.definitionFit: To globe-trot is to travel widely around the world, visiting many countries.

clue.text: Horseplay in back of cafe and waiters doubly sapped of energy

indicators.note: energy has a one-letter abbreviation, and doubly sapped means it is removed twice over
the back of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: Waiters in a cafe are worn out after fooling about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waiters' means people waiting, not table staff. Equus is Peter Shaffer's play about a boy who blinds horses.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as horse play, this is a stage play centred on horses, and the title is Latin for horse.

clue.text: A stud excited about American woman associated with modelling

indicators.note: about means going around, so the shuffled letters surround the next piece
excited means stirred up, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: US is the standard abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: A man gets worked up over an American fashion model.
explanation.walkthrough: Modelling suggests fashion; it is sculpting in wax.
explanation.definitionFit: Madame Tussaud made wax figures and founded the famous London museum of waxworks.

clue.text: Traitor present, not to be trusted

indicators.note: a word not to be trusted cannot be taken at face value, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A betrayer is in the room and cannot be relied upon.
explanation.definitionFit: A serpent is a treacherous, deceitful person, from the snake in Eden.
